次中音薩魯梭風主要採用黃銅或其他金屬材質製成共鳴管體和音孔結構，提供溫暖厚重的音: The tenor sarrusophone is made mainly with a brass or other metal tube and tone-hole structure, which gives a warm, heavy tone as its base. The mouthpiece is a double-reed design, usually of cane, similar to the reeds of the saxophone or the oboe. The inside of the metal tube is precisely worked to secure accurate tuning and tone. The keywork uses a precise system of metal springs and rods, which makes complex fingering manageable. The whole combines the solidity of a brass instrument with the expressiveness of a double-reed instrument.

It was mainly used in French military bands and wind bands from the late nineteenth to the early twentieth century. As modern band line-ups changed, the number of works written for it stayed limited. Some French composers wrote parts for the sarrusophone family in wind band scores, but the sources do not record specific representative works. Today the instrument is kept in production mainly by special order, and is used mostly in historical instrument revival performance or specialist study.
次中音薩魯梭風是薩魯梭風家族中的次中音成員，屬於金屬雙簧片風樂器，音高為降B調，: The tenor sarrusophone is the tenor member of the sarrusophone family, a metal double-reed wind instrument pitched in B flat, with the same range as the tenor saxophone. These instruments were originally made from the late nineteenth to the early twentieth century by Orsi, Gautrot and his successor Couesnon, and by the Evette & Schaeffer company (now Buffet Crampon). Today only Orsi makes them, to special order.
次中音薩魯梭風起源於19世紀末的法國，由樂器製造商奧西首先研發。這種金屬雙簧片風: The tenor sarrusophone originated in France at the end of the nineteenth century, and was first developed by the instrument maker Orsi. This metal double-reed wind instrument was meant to fill a gap in tone in the band, offering a warmer, heavier quality than the saxophone. Gautrot, Couesnon and other makers then took up production, and it gradually spread through European wind bands. In the early twentieth century the Evette & Schaeffer company (now Buffet Crampon) also began making the instrument, which widened its use further. Although it had some reputation in military bands and wind bands at the time, the changing band line-ups of the mid twentieth century gradually pushed the tenor sarrusophone aside. Today only the Orsi company continues to make it to special order, which makes it a comparatively rare classical instrument.
次中音薩魯梭風音色深沉而富有力度，具有獨特的銅管樂器般的溫暖質感，兼具雙簧片樂器: The tenor sarrusophone has a deep, forceful timbre with a warmth peculiar to brass instruments, combined with the expressiveness of a double-reed instrument. In the low register it is heavy and steady, in the middle it is warm with a slightly nasal cast, and towards the top it grows brighter and more penetrating. Compared with the soft, round tenor saxophone, the sarrusophone is firmer and thicker, with an old and nostalgic quality. Its metal resonating body lets the sound waves vibrate fully and produces a deep resonance, which gives it a distinctive presence in a band. On the whole the tenor sarrusophone keeps the solemnity of a classical wind instrument without losing a voice-like expressiveness.
